query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy nanoalloys, a kinetically trapped short‐range chemical order—established during rapid synthesis—mediates the local electronic structure such that atomic diffusion and phase segregation are suppressed at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy nanoalloy nanoparticles produced via a fast, laser-induced thermionic emission reduction method, yielding uniformly mixed particles (≈1–3 nm) on a carbonaceous support.
generation.intervention: Thermal annealing in an inert atmosphere over a high-temperature range (e.g., 673 K to 1073 K).
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment where diffusion becomes activated (around 0.5–0.6 Tm) but oxidation is minimized; nanoparticles remain below ~5 nm in size and possess near equimolar composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Short‐range chemical order (SRO) which reflects a uniform distribution of multiple metal atoms and an associated electronic structure stabilized by the specific valence electron concentration.
generation.mechanism: The rapid synthesis process locks in a metastable, well-mixed atomic configuration with pronounced SRO. This SRO, in turn, tailors the local bond environments and electronic density such that the diffusion of atoms is hindered, reducing the thermodynamic drive for phase separation even when high-temperature conditions would normally promote atomic rearrangement.
generation.predicted_outcome: After high-temperature annealing, fast-synthesized nanoalloys will maintain a single-phase, uniform elemental distribution with minimal phase segregation compared to slower-synthesized counterparts.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloys produced via conventional slower synthesis methods, which are expected to show more significant phase segregation or chemical inhomogeneity under similar annealing conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction applies to nanoparticles with sizes below ~5 nm and nearly equimolar compositions; the effect may differ for larger or compositionally skewed particles or under conditions where oxidation or other extrinsic factors dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of the inherent electronic structure effects versus kinetic trapping to stability remain to be precisely determined and may be sensitive to synthesis parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloys: one using the rapid laser-induced synthesis method and one with a conventional slower method. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing (e.g., at 800 K) under an inert atmosphere. Characterize the phase structure, elemental distribution, and short-range order using X-ray diffraction, in situ transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.
measurements: XRD for phase identification and peak broadening trends
TEM imaging to assess microstructural evolution and the presence of segregated phases
Measurements of diffusion rates via tracer techniques (if applicable)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the rapidly synthesized and conventionally synthesized nanoalloys display similar levels of phase segregation or loss of uniform elemental distribution after annealing, or if the rapid synthesis sample fails to retain enhanced short-range order relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis—linking kinetic trapping and SRO to high-temperature stability—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Diffusion involving atom transport from one location to another governs many important processes and behaviors such as precipitation and phase nucleation. The inherent chemical complexity in compositionally complex materials poses challenges for modeling atomic diffusion and the resulting formation of chemically ordered structures. Here, we introduce a neural network kinetics (NNK) scheme that predicts and simulates diffusion-induced chemical and structural evolution in complex concentrated chemical environments. The framework is grounded on efficient on-lattice structure and chemistry representation combined with artificial neural networks, enabling precise prediction of all path-dependent migration barriers and individual atom jumps. To demonstrate the method, we study the temperature-dependent local chemical ordering in a refractory NbMoTa alloy and reveal a critical temperature at which the B2 order reaches a maximum. The atomic jump randomness map exhibits the highest diffusion heterogeneity (multiplicity) in the vicinity of this characteristic temperature, which is closely related to chemical ordering and B2 structure formation. It is found from the RBA calculations that competition between the FCC and B2 phases starts at valence electron concentration, n ≈ 8. Comparison with the present experimental data for CCFN-Al0.5 (n = 7.67) where FCC peaks are indicated in XRD (Fig. IIc), shows that the RBA model may overestimate the stability of the B2 phase. However, in comparison with a new HEA composition, AlCoCrFeNi2.1, where the corresponding valence electron concentration is n = 7.70, the experimental observation of an FCC/B2 dual-phase constitution. Furthermore, experimental evidence of B2 presence has also been reported in CCFN-Al0.75, CCFN-Al1, and CCFN-Al1.5 with n values ranging from 6.57 to 7.41. These observations not only validate our theoretical prediction but also demonstrate that the formation of B2 phase is strongly correlated with the short-range chemical order between Al and the excess composition of Ni transition metals in the HEAs, suggesting possible effects of the processing method and cooling rate, as noted by Dahlborg et al..

Metal nanoalloys are critical catalysts and widely used in many chemical reactions ranging from environmental to energy fields (). Conventional bottom-up routes, such as wet-chemistry methods for the synthesis of metal nanoalloys, usually need to consider the miscibility of each metallic element in the phase diagrams to avoid the phase segregation during the formation of the particles (). The immiscible issue of metals restricts the realm of nanoalloys and precludes the discovery of new nanoalloys with superior functionalities (). In recent years, high-entropy nanoalloys (HENAs) containing equal stoichiometric ratios of various metals in each particle in a well-mixed manner have attracted a lot of interest because of their unusual physical and chemical properties. These unique properties make them attractive as catalysts (), such as oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) that has great potential for applications in energy and environmental science. Recent studies have revealed that the slow reaction kinetics in traditional methods is one of the major obstacles that lead to the phase segregation in nanoalloys (, ).
